claims.text: A bank statement provides a formal summary of financial activity for a specific account over a defined timeframe.
Financial institutions generally do not allow changes to be made to a statement once it has been issued to the client.
Customers often use statements to track their spending, identify potential fraud, and reconcile their accounts.
Many banks provide unofficial transaction history tools that allow customers to monitor their account activity between the issuance of official statements.
Open banking allows account holders to authorize third-party financial institutions to view their account balances.
Since banks began using computers in the 1960s, statements have typically been issued on a monthly basis.
Some financial institutions use the mailing of statements as an opportunity to distribute promotional materials or notify customers of fee and interest rate adjustments.
Some banks have begun charging fees for paper statements to encourage customers to switch to electronic alternatives.
In Japan, there is no historical tradition of mailing bank statements, as customers typically track their own balances using passbooks at ATMs.
Electronic statements are frequently generated in PDF format to make unauthorized alterations more difficult.
While electronic statements eliminate the risk of physical theft, they can be more susceptible to computer fraud or data interception.
A bank statement reflects the bank's perspective on an account, meaning that credit and debit entries appear reversed compared to how a depositor would record them as an asset.
The transaction details appearing on a bank statement might differ from the actual consumer-facing name of a business.
Visa provides specific instructions regarding how merchant name fields should identify the acceptance entity and the underlying seller when using payment facilitators or marketplaces.

In the United Kingdom, banks and building societies are legally obligated to provide statements on paper or other durable media, with exceptions for passbook holders, online-only bank customers, and those who have opted out of paper statements.
United States banks are only mandated to issue a checking account statement if the account has recorded at least one transaction during the month.
Bank statements are frequently used to verify authenticity for purposes like auditing, lending, and financial checks.
The prevalence of digital bank statements in formats like PDF has increased the focus on verification and document consistency.
Since the early 2010s, some mortgage lenders have offered programs that utilize bank deposit history to evaluate borrower income instead of relying on traditional pay stubs or tax returns.
Income assessment programs based on bank deposits are typically targeted at self-employed individuals or those with nontraditional income.
